cards.title: Avatar vs. Demographic: The Empty-Nester Test
cards.summary: Why 'women 45+' is a demographic, not an avatar, and the specific-context standard that separates them.
cards.use_when: You are about to write ad copy, a VSL or a landing page and want to check whether you actually know who you are writing to.
steps: Test your avatar by pausing and riffing for 30 seconds on: exactly who they are, their hopes and dreams, their current situation, the problem they face, and what they would wish for if they could snap their fingers. If you cannot do this, do more research before writing.

Treat age and gender as a starting demographic only, not an avatar. The source's example: 'women 45 and up with cats' is a gender and an age; it says nothing about fears, dreams or how they describe the problem to a friend at 2 a.m.

Build a specific person carrying situational and emotional context. The source's model avatar is Margaret, 55, on her third cat, an empty nester after her husband passed and her kids moved 2,000 miles away; she has already lost two cats to chronic kidney disease, has tried fountains, different water bowls and adding water to food, and is anxious and paranoid about losing the third.

Include what the avatar has tried and what fails. The source argues struggling ads usually trace back to not understanding the avatar well enough, so unanswered failed-solution history is a signal to keep researching.
Every avatar in your library should carry quoted evidence, a trigger moment and a job statement before you use it for creative work.
caveats: The source's $10k/day framing comes from a paid-community marketer selling a drop-shipping course; treat scale claims as his positioning, not a benchmark.
Translating avatar language into hooks and scripts belongs in a later creative module; this card is only about the avatar definition.

cards.title: 60-Minute Manual Research Sprint: 80/20 Reddit and Amazon
cards.summary: The source's one-hour protocol: 30 minutes on public forums and 30 minutes on Amazon reviews, manually copying verbatim text.
cards.use_when: You have picked a demographic and need to build a real avatar without defaulting to AI-generated personas.
steps: Pick the starting demographic from the top customer demographic of your largest competitor, using tools like SimilarWeb, another spy tool, or asking a chatbot, so research is aimed at a plausible buyer profile.

Block 60 minutes total. Spend roughly 80% on public discussion forums (Reddit and niche forums) and 20% on Amazon reviews. The source says Reddit is the largest public discussion library for understanding an avatar.

For the 30 forum minutes, adopt the avatar's mind state: literally sit as that person and search the problem in their words, e.g. 'my cat won't drink water Reddit' or 'hair loss making me less attractive Reddit'.
Open a Google Doc as your research library. Copy-paste whole comments and posts, then bold or underline emotional language, failed solutions, situational details and repeated phrases.
Read the comment sections, not just the original posts; the source finds the strongest material in replies and in confession-oriented subreddits where people admit insecurities.
Repeat for 30 minutes on Amazon reviews of competing products, harvesting the same categories: fears, desired outcomes, emotional mind states and previously tried solutions.
If you cannot spare an hour in one sitting, spread it across multiple days, but complete the hour before writing copy.
caveats: This is a manual-first protocol; the source still says AI tools like Gemini or Claude have unmatched efficiency and detail once you already understand your avatar.
The method is universal but the 80/20 forum-to-review split is the presenter's recommendation, not a measured law.

cards.title: Search Query Craft for Avatar Research
cards.summary: How to write search queries as the avatar to surface the rawest forum threads on their problem.
cards.use_when: You are starting the forum half of a manual research sprint and need to find threads worth mining.
steps: Write queries as the avatar searching for help, not as a marketer searching for topics. Examples from the source: 'my cat won't drink water please help Reddit', 'how do I get my cat to drink more water Reddit', 'my cat refuses to drink water'.
Include the problem's emotional phrasing when relevant, e.g. 'straight up hair loss making me less attractive Reddit'.
Add demographic or identity qualifiers to sharpen the avatar, e.g. adding 'men' or 'ask men over 30' when researching men 30-50 with hair loss.
Read threads word for word within a timed block and let the vocabulary guide the next query; one thread usually reveals adjacent phrasings and subreddits worth searching.
Prioritise confession-heavy communities such as 'off my chest' where people describe the problem in extreme emotional detail, since these give the rawest mind-state language.
caveats: The source's specific example queries are for a cat kidney product and a hair-restoration product; substitute your own category's problem statements rather than copying them.
Search-engine behaviour and subreddit availability change, so verify what surfaces for your niche rather than assuming these exact queries still return the same threads.

cards.title: Copy Verbatim and Bold: Building the Language Library
cards.summary: The mechanical habit of pasting raw quotes into a doc and marking emotional language, failed solutions and situational context.
cards.use_when: You are in a research session and need a repeatable way to capture material you can actually write from.
steps: Paste whole posts and comments rather than paraphrasing; the source says there is no real structure to the doc, just copy-paste with spacing between entries.
Bold or underline phrases and keywords that stand out: emotional language, named failed solutions, demographic detail and self-descriptions.
Screenshots are acceptable and often efficient when a post is dense with material, but bold or underline text when you want it findable later.

Preserve exact wording including harsh or self-deprecating phrasing. The source's example: write 'do you hate and feel like your balding is making you look uglier', not a sanitised 'are you tired of looking worse'.
Tag each pasted block implicitly by where it came from, so you can return to the thread later for comments you skipped.
Run this continuously while the timer runs; the point is volume of authentic language, and after 30 focused minutes the source claims copy starts to write itself.
caveats: The source's advice to use the avatar's own words including insults is about authenticity, not about harassing customers; use judgement on what is ethical to reflect back.
Do not attribute a single Reddit comment to your whole audience; it is one data point, and the method relies on repetition across many threads.

cards.title: Emotional Mind States: Frustration vs. Fear
cards.summary: Identify the dominant emotion behind the problem because each mind state needs different copy.
cards.use_when: You have raw research and need to decide the emotional register your ads should use.
steps: While researching, explicitly log whether the avatar feels guilt, embarrassment, shame, frustration, fear, anxiety or depression about the situation.

Ask which emotion dominates for this avatar. The source contrasts drop shippers hitting failed tests, whose primary emotion is frustration, with an empty nester protecting a pet, whose primary emotion is fear, anxiety and possibly depression.
Adapt the copy register to the emotion: frustration copy can call out wasted effort and broken promises, while fear copy should speak to loss, worst-case outcomes and protection.

Use the documented worst-case moment as your emotional anchor. In the hair-loss example the source singles out one man's account of a friend pointing out his hair loss condescendingly in a room full of staring people while he was already depressed, and says he would write ad copy from that one instance alone.
Re-check your current ads against the logged mind state and cut copy that addresses a different emotion than the one the research shows.
caveats: Emotional register and claims must stay within ad-platform policies and honest representation; the source's vivid fear framing is a copy technique, not permission to exaggerate outcomes.
The source is describing a marketing course audience and a pet supplement example; verify the dominant emotion in your own niche rather than assuming it transfers.
cards.source_name: How I Find Avatars That Scale Facebook Ads to $10k_day.docx

cards.title: Mine Named Failed Solutions, Not Generic Categories
cards.summary: Extract the exact products and procedures the avatar already tried so copy can name them specifically.
cards.use_when: You are writing hooks or objection-handling copy and want to reference failed prior attempts credibly.
steps: While reading forums and reviews, capture every named product, drug, procedure or workaround the avatar mentions failing with.
Replace generic categories with specific names in copy. The source's example from hair loss: do not write 'have you tried hair supplements or drugs', write 'have you tried minoxidil'.

Capture the cost and extensiveness of failed solutions. In the hair-loss research, a forum user described spending $6,500 on Neograft for the front and $5,000 for the crown with a rebuild-per-section process, framing it as roughly $300 a month.
For low-cost workarounds like cat hydration, capture the specific variants tried, e.g. fountains, different water bowls and adding water to food.
Use the named failures to position the offer against what the avatar has already rejected, since the source treats failed-solution history as part of the avatar record.
caveats: Named competitor or medical solutions should be referenced factually; do not invent efficacy comparisons the research does not support.
Price figures quoted by forum users are anecdotes, not verified market pricing.
cards.source_name: How I Find Avatars That Scale Facebook Ads to $10k_day.docx

cards.title: Understanding Before Curiosity: How to Build a Hook
cards.summary: Curiosity-driven hooks fail alone; pair deep understanding of the avatar's situation with attention-grabbing phrasing.
cards.use_when: You are writing hook lines and want to avoid clever-but-empty angles that make the avatar roll their eyes.
steps: Diagnose the common beginner trap: turning a claim into a curiosity hook and assuming it converts. The source's example 'the easiest way to drop ship is not what you think' drives curiosity but fails to make the avatar feel understood, so the target audience rolls their eyes.

Start from the current situation and deepest fear, then add curiosity mechanics on top. The cat example: 'Two women whose cats don't drink water. It seems innocent but could be the reason you lose your last companion a few years too early.'

Identify the situational call-out ('two women whose cats don't drink water'), the curiosity element ('it seems innocent'), the deepest fear (losing the companion early) and the identity-specific language ('last companion' signalling empty nesters).
Replace generic pain-point hooks such as 'are you tired of this pain point' plus a product claim with copy that articulates the avatar's situation in their own words.
Ground the hook in specific mechanics your audience actually recognises. The source's own course example cites '$200 CPMs and $5 CPCs on launch day' rather than the vague 'my product test failed'.
caveats: The source's framing 'people buy when they feel understood' is his opinion, supported by example, not a measured conversion law.
Hook creation and script writing belong downstream in a creative module; this card covers only the understanding required before writing them.

cards.title: Use AI as a Supplement, Not a Substitute for Research
cards.summary: The source's argument for manual research first: AI is efficient but becomes a crutch when you do not know what you are looking for.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to run deep-research prompts instead of doing forum and review mining yourself.
steps: Acknowledge the tool's real strength: the source explicitly says AI tools such as Gemini, ChatGPT and Claude have unmatched efficiency and level of detail.

Delay heavy AI use while you are still learning what to look for. The source says if you are just starting out, do not use it yet, because you will mistake polished output for genuine avatar understanding.
Avoid the trap of running a deep-research prompt and assuming you now understand the avatar. The source compares it to answering emails and feeling productive without moving the needle.
Do a manual research sprint first, then use AI to accelerate work you can already evaluate, since an LLM is only as good as the inputs the operator provides.

Audit current AI-written copy against your manual research. The source claims you will find lines that are off-base: not what the customer wants, not how they describe the problem, not the emotions they feel.
caveats: This is a strong opinion from a marketer who sells community access, and it is framed as a starting-out rule; experienced operators may get value from AI-assisted research with strong inputs.
The source does not claim manual research is superior to AI in efficiency or detail, only in building genuine understanding.
cards.source_name: How I Find Avatars That Scale Facebook Ads to $10k_day.docx

cards.title: Avatar Record Requirements: Quotes, Trigger, Job
cards.summary: The minimum contents any avatar must have in your library before it is usable for creative work.
cards.use_when: You are cataloguing research into avatar records or auditing whether an existing avatar is complete.
steps: Include quoted evidence from real sources so the avatar is traceable to what people actually wrote, not to your paraphrase.
Record a trigger moment: the specific situation that starts the search or purchase, such as a friend's comment about hair loss in front of others, or a cat refusing water.
Write a job statement capturing what progress the avatar wants, not just the demographic fields.
Capture specific situational context rather than broad life stages, e.g. the source's example of a 55-year-old empty nester with her third cat rather than 'women 45 and up'.

Capture procedural and category vocabulary exactly: 'Neograft rebuilding the front and crown' and 'minoxidil' rather than 'transplants and drugs', or 'fountains and water bowls' rather than 'hydration products'.
Note vernacular differences between avatars, since the source's method hinges on exact phrasing rather than a generic persona template.
caveats: The source warns against persona templates with demographic fields and no job, such as '30+ year old woman with knee pain'; those should not count as avatars.
A quoted line from one forum user may not represent the whole demographic; consolidate multiple sources into the record.
cards.source_name: How I Find Avatars That Scale Facebook Ads to $10k_day.docx

cards.title: Research Before Scaling: The $10k-Day Premise and Its Limits
cards.summary: The source's argument that avatar clarity gates scaling, framed with its commercial context and limitations.
cards.use_when: You are deciding how much research effort to invest before spending on ads or scaling a proven offer.
steps: Accept the source's premise that if you struggle to write winning ads, it is likely because you do not know and understand your avatar well enough.
Set research intensity against ambition: the source says a $1k day still requires an avatar, but claims a shot at $10,000 days requires knowing the avatar deeply.
Apply the research to the formats you actually run. The source connects manual avatar research to his long-form Facebook ad copy with native images, and says the same applies to VSLs.
Run the comparison test: after a manual research sprint, read your current copy and look for lines that miss what the customer wants, how they describe the problem, or what they actually feel.
Use the gaps found in that comparison as the improvement list for your next tests, then judge the method by your own testing and scaling results.
caveats: The presenter is selling a drop-shipping course and community and uses $10,000 days as marketing framing; results are his example, not a promise for your account.
No specific spend, testing budget, timeframe or statistical benchmark is given, so do not treat the scale claims as a forecast.
cards.source_name: How I Find Avatars That Scale Facebook Ads to $10k_day.docx

cards.title: Pre-Existing Insecurity Changes How You Write
cards.summary: Segment avatars by whether the problem stacks on top of existing confidence issues, because the copy register differs.
cards.use_when: You are drafting copy for a problem where some buyers are already confident and others are not.
steps: Look for self-descriptions in the research that reveal baseline confidence. The source's hair-loss example quotes a man turning 31, single, a bit chubby, with self-confidence and self-esteem issues who says his hair gives him a confidence boost.
Treat the compounding case differently: for someone already unconfident, hair loss stacks on top of existing insecurity rather than being a standalone problem.
Write differently to the already-confident avatar, who has life 'put together' and starts balding, versus the unconfident avatar for whom the loss accelerates an existing struggle.

Capture repeated preference statements that reveal the comparison the avatar makes. In the source's research, multiple forum participants said it is better to be bald than balding, i.e. avoid 'no man's land'.
Use the avatar's own framing of how others perceive them, e.g. worry that receding hairlines look unappealing to women 25 and older, rather than abstract attractiveness claims.
caveats: These are quotes from individual forum users in one niche; verify that the same stacking dynamic exists in your category before building a segment around it.
Sensitive appearance and dating insecurities require careful, non-exploitative creative; the source's technique is about authenticity, not amplifying shame.
